content.title: About
content.content: Clementine is a hybrid of mandarin (Citrus reticulata) and pomelo (Citrus maxima) first created in the early 20th century. The sweet, juicy fruits have a thin, easy‑to‑peel skin, few seeds, and bright orange flesh. Clementines are usually eaten fresh, but they also work well in salads, desserts, and drinks.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “clementine” honors Saint Clement, the patron saint of sailors, because early shipments arrived via the Mediterranean Sea.
Unlike most mandarins, clementines are virtually seed‑free, making them kid‑friendly.
Clementines ripen in winter (December‑February), earning them the nickname “winter citrus.”
The peel is rich in essential oils used in aromatherapy and for zesting.
In California, clementines are one of the most popular fruits during the holiday season.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: One clementine provides over 50 % of the daily recommended vitamin C, supporting immunity and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of flavonoids
items.content: Flavonoids act as antioxidants, helping protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium aids in maintaining fluid balance and proper heart function.

items.title: Low‑calorie fruit
items.content: A single clementine contains about 35 kcal, making it a weight‑friendly snack.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber in the flesh promotes regular bowel movements and helps prevent constipation.

items.title: Citrus allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to citrus fruits, including skin itching, swelling, or gastrointestinal symptoms.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The high acidity can irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcer disease.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: As with many fruits, clementines may carry pesticide residues; washing thoroughly before eating is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Eat clementines fresh by cutting them in half and squeezing out the juice or eating the segments. They can be added to fruit salads, yogurt, smoothies, baked goods, and sauces. The zest is used to flavor desserts and drinks.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store clementines at room temperature for up to 1 week. For longer storage (2‑3 weeks), keep them in the refrigerator’s fruit drawer. Avoid storing with highly perishable fruits to prevent accelerated ripening.

noodles-with-vegetables-in-tomato-based-.title: Noodles with vegetables in tomato-based sauce, diet frozen meal

content.title: About
content.content: Noodles with vegetables in tomato-based sauce is a diet frozen meal designed for quick and convenient nutrition. It contains whole‑grain noodles, carrots, broccoli, bell pepper and a low‑fat tomato sauce. Ideal for those monitoring their calorie intake.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The meal is ready in 3–5 minutes using a microwave or stovetop.
The tomato sauce is enriched with lycopene, a powerful antioxidant.
Vegetables are flash‑frozen to preserve vitamins and minerals.
The product can be gluten‑free when made with gluten‑free noodles (specified on the label).
Each serving provides about 250 kcal, making it suitable for diet plans.

items.title: Low calorie content
items.content: A modest calorie count helps maintain energy balance during weight loss.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetables and whole‑grain noodles supply fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Tomatoes, carrots and broccoli provide vitamin C, vitamin A, potassium and iron.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Lycopene in the tomato sauce helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin C and other phytochemicals contribute to a stronger immune system.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: The product may contain traces of soy, milk or gluten; individuals with these allergies should check the label.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The tomato sauce contains a moderate amount of salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Not suitable for children under 3
items.content: The noodle texture may be difficult for very young children; recommended for ages 3 and up.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Microwave the sealed package for 2–3 minutes or place the contents in a saucepan with a splash of water, bring to a boil and simmer 4–5 minutes, stirring occasionally. Serve hot, optionally garnish with fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen meal at –18 °C or lower. Once thawed, cook immediately and do not store at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

pizza-with-cheese-and-extra-vegetables-t.title: Pizza with cheese and extra vegetables, thin crust

content.title: About
content.content: A thin-crust pizza topped with melted cheese, fresh vegetables (bell pepper, onion, mushrooms, olives) and aromatic herbs. The dough is made from high‑quality flour, giving it a crisp and light texture. Perfect as a light lunch or dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Thin crust is baked at high temperature, creating a characteristic crunch.
The cheese is usually mozzarella, which melts into a stretchy layer.
Vegetables are added just before the end of baking to keep their color and bite.
The tradition of thin pizza comes from Naples, where it is called “pizza romana”.
The cheese‑vegetable combination boosts the dish with B‑vitamins and vitamin C.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Mozzarella provides calcium, essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Vitamins and antioxidants
items.content: Bell pepper, onion and mushrooms supply vitamin C, vitamin A and antioxidants.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Thin crust and moderate cheese make this pizza less calorie‑dense than traditional versions.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetables and whole‑grain flour in the dough support digestion and satiety.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Mozzarella and mushrooms add dairy and plant protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cheese may cause discomfort for people who cannot digest lactose.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to dairy cheese.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Salt used in the dough and sauce can be high; those with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional crust contains gluten, making it unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pizza hot, cut into slices. Optionally drizzle with extra‑virgin olive oil or sprinkle fresh basil. Pairs well with a light salad or a glass of dry white wine.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to restore the crisp crust.
